newsitem.title: USA: Rail unions in unity pact on Conrail merger.
newsitem.headline: Rail unions in unity pact on Conrail merger.

text.p: Unions representing about 70,000 workers at Conrail and its two suitors said Wednesday they had agreed to jointly analyse the competing rail merger proposals and emerge with a unified position.

The unprecedented stance taken by a dozen rail unions, the AFL-CIO and its Transportation Trades Department serves notice on Conrail, CSX Corp., Norfolk Southern Corp. and investors that labour intends to take an active and unified role in the unfolding merger drama.

"We will analyse the competing bids for Conrail and determine the best course for labour in the latest of a series of mammoth rail mergers," John Sweeney, president of the 78-union AFL-CIO, said in a statement.
"We will be looking at the effects on employees, competition, shippers, communities and the financial health of the railroad industry," Sweeney said in a statement.

Conrail and CSX have entered into an $8.4 billion merger pact, but Norfolk Southern Corp. jumped in last week with an $8.8 billion bid and filed suit to try to stop the Conrail-CSX deal. The railroad giants are now wrangling in court.

Ed Wytkind, executive director of the AFL-CIO's Transportation Trades Department, said the unions do not have a timetable for coming up with a unified position on the merger, but said they were aware that time was growing short.
"We're going to try to do our initial analysis of this merger as quickly as we can," he said. "We know that they (Conrail and CSX) plan to file a formal plan of merger in January."

Although the merger will be decided by shareholders, regulators and perhaps the courts, a unified labour front could wield considerable clout with regulatory agencies and in Congress, especially if job losses are threatened.
Further, the agreement binds the unions to bargain with the carriers under the umbrella of the Transportation Trades Department, instead of cutting separate deals, Wytkind said.

"This is a pretty historic move because it basically sends a signal to Washington and to Wall Street and to everyone else that we intend to stick together as a labour movement," said Wytkind. "And there will not be any individual negotiations."

The decision to form a unified front on the merger was instigated by Sweeney and AFL-CIO Secretary-Treasurer Richard Trumka, who have sought to reactivite the labour movement in the past year, especially as a social and political force.
Separately, the chairman of the House Transportation Committee said a hearing set for next month on a possible acquisition of Conrail will focus on the government's action in the proceeding.
